paper.title: Mock Paper · Primary 3 Language Use and Comprehension (C)
paper.note: The third of three Primary 3 papers. Same length and marks, but the comprehension passage is non-narrative — information rather than a story — which schools do set at Primary 3. Sit this one closest to the exam.

questions.q: Neither of the boys ______ able to find the missing key.
Please put the scissors back ______ the drawer.
My cousin ______ in Melbourne since last March.
That is the man ______ dog barks all night.
The baby fell asleep ______ the music was still playing.
We have been waiting at this bus stop ______ twenty minutes.
Hurry up, ______ we will be late for the concert.
The teacher told us ______ quietly in the corridor.
This bag is ______ than that one, but it costs more.
______ of the two answers do you think is correct?

sections.name: Booklet A · Vocabulary
sections.instruction: Choose the word or phrase closest in meaning to the word in bold.

questions.q: The path was **slippery** after the heavy rain.
Mei Ling **glanced** at the clock and gasped.
The kitten was **timid** and hid behind the sofa.
Grandfather **mended** my kite with tape and a stick.

sections.name: Booklet B · Grammar Cloze
sections.instruction: Fill each blank with one suitable word.
sections.passage:
The Night the Lights Went Out

It happened at ten past eight, (1)______ we were in the middle of dinner. The fan stopped first, and then every light in the flat went out at once.

My little sister screamed. My mother laughed and told her there was (2)______ to be afraid of.

My father felt his way to the kitchen drawer, (3)______ he kept a torch for exactly this reason. Unfortunately the batteries (4)______ flat, because nobody had checked them since the year before.

In the end we lit two candles and put them on saucers in the middle of the table. The rice had gone cold, (5)______ none of us minded.

We stayed there for almost an hour. My grandmother told us about the kampong she grew up (6)______, where the lights went out so often that nobody bothered to complain.

The power came back at nine o'clock, and the flat suddenly looked very bright and very ordinary. My sister, (7)______ had screamed at the beginning, asked whether we could turn the lights off again.

It is the (8)______ interesting dinner we have had all year.

answers.tip: A time word is needed to join the two actions.
'There was nothing to be afraid of' — the usual phrase.
'Where' points back to the drawer, the place the torch was kept.
'Batteries' is plural and the story is in the past.
The two halves disagree, so a contrast word is needed.
'The kampong she grew up in' — 'grow up in' a place.
'Who' stands for my sister, a person, and is the subject of 'had screamed'.
'The most interesting' — longer adjectives take 'most', not '-est'.

sections.name: Booklet B · Spelling and Grammar Editing
sections.instruction: There is one spelling or grammar error in each line. Write the correction — one word only.

questions.q: My class have a new pet last month.
questions.tip: The error was “have”. “Last month” is in the past.

questions.q: It is a rabbit with white fur and one brown ears.
questions.tip: The error was “ears”. “One” means a single ear.

questions.q: Mrs Tan keep it in a wooden hutch beside the window.
questions.tip: The error was “keep”. “Mrs Tan” is singular, so the verb takes an -s.

questions.q: We taked turns to feed it every morning.
questions.tip: The error was “taked”. The past tense of “take” is “took”.

questions.q: The rabbit likes carrots more than any other vegetible.
questions.tip: The error was “vegetible”. It is spelt “vegetable”.

questions.q: On Monday Hui Ling forgetted to close the hutch door.
questions.tip: The error was “forgetted”. The past tense of “forget” is “forgot”.

questions.q: The rabbit hopped out and hidded under the cupboard.
questions.tip: The error was “hidded”. The past tense of “hide” is “hid”.

questions.q: We was very worried that it would escape into the corridor.
Ravi lay on the floor and reach for it with a carrot.
questions.tip: The error was “reach”. The rest of the sentence is in the past.

questions.q: Nobody have forgotten since that day.

sections.name: Booklet B · Comprehension
sections.instruction: Read the passage and answer the questions. Note the marks for each question.
sections.passage:
Why Spiders Are Not Insects

Most people call a spider an insect. It is an easy mistake to make, and it is wrong.

An insect has six legs. A spider has eight. If you have the patience to count them, that is the quickest test there is.

There are other differences. An insect's body is in three parts: a head, a middle part and a back part. A spider's body is in two. An insect usually has wings, and a spider never does. Most insects have two feelers on the head, called antennae, and spiders have none at all.

Scientists put spiders in a group called arachnids. Scorpions and ticks belong to the same group.

Spiders are useful. A single spider in a garden may eat two thousand insects in a year, including mosquitoes that carry disease. Farmers in some countries welcome them for this reason.

Not all spiders build webs. The jumping spider has no web at all. It has excellent eyesight and simply creeps up on its meal, then leaps, sometimes fifty times the length of its own body.

Spider silk is remarkable. It is thinner than a human hair, and for its weight it is stronger than steel. Scientists have been trying for years to copy it in a factory, and so far nobody has managed it.

So the next time somebody points at a spider and calls it an insect, you may count the legs.

questions.q: What do most people wrongly call a spider?
What does the writer say is the quickest way to tell a spider from an insect?
questions.a: Counting the legs: an insect has six and a spider has eight.

questions.q: Give two differences between a spider's body and an insect's body, apart from the legs.
questions.a: Any two of: an insect's body is in three parts and a spider's in two; an insect usually has wings and a spider never does; most insects have two antennae and spiders have none.

questions.q: Why do farmers in some countries welcome spiders?
questions.a: Because a single spider may eat two thousand insects in a year, including mosquitoes that carry disease.

questions.q: How does a jumping spider catch its food?
questions.a: It has no web. It uses its excellent eyesight to creep up on its meal and then leaps at it, sometimes fifty times its own body length.

questions.q: Give two facts about spider silk from the passage.
questions.a: Any two of: it is thinner than a human hair; for its weight it is stronger than steel; scientists have been trying for years to copy it and nobody has managed it yet.

questions.q: Which word in the passage means 'very unusual and worth noticing'?
The writer says calling a spider an insect is 'an easy mistake to make'. Why is it easy to make?
questions.a: Spiders look very like insects — both are small many-legged creatures found in the same places — so people group them together without counting the legs or the body parts.

questions.q: What does the writer want the reader to do at the end of the passage, and why?
questions.a: To count the legs when somebody calls a spider an insect. It is the simplest test, and it lets the reader settle the question for himself rather than taking anybody's word for it.

questions.q: Do you think the writer admires spiders? Give one reason from the passage.
questions.a: Yes. Any one of: he calls them useful and says they eat mosquitoes that carry disease; he calls their silk remarkable and stronger than steel for its weight; he points out that scientists still cannot copy it.
